title: Blood groups and transfusions
examples: Why is it important to check blood types before a transfusion?
What happens if my blood type does not match the donor's?
Can you explain what antigens are on red blood cells?

explain.say: Today we are learning about blood groups and safe transfusions.

draw.text: Blood Groups: A, B, AB, O

explain.say: Some people have antigens on their red blood cells.
Blood type A has A antigens on its cells.
Blood type B has B antigens on its cells.
Blood type AB has both A and B antigens.

draw.text: Type AB: Has A and B antigens

explain.say: Blood type O has neither A nor B antigens.

draw.text: Type O: No A or B antigens

faq.q: Why do blood groups need to match for a transfusion?
faq.a: If the donor's blood has antigens that match the recipient's existing antibodies, it can cause a reaction. This is because the recipient's body might attack the foreign antigens. You might also hear this called 'immune reaction' or 'blood incompatibility'.
asks: What happens if I get the wrong blood?
Why can't I take blood from anyone?

faq.q: Which blood type is the universal donor?
faq.a: Blood type O is considered the universal donor because its red blood cells lack A and B antigens. This means they are less likely to trigger a major reaction in the recipient. Other ways to ask this are: 'Which blood type is safe for everyone?' or 'What blood type has no antigens?'
asks: What blood type can go to anyone?

faq.q: Which blood type is the universal recipient?
faq.a: Blood type AB is the universal recipient because it has both A and B antigens. This means it can safely receive blood from any other blood type. You could also ask: 'What blood type can take blood from everyone?'
asks: What blood type can receive any blood?
Is AB the best type to receive?

faq.a: Antigens are specific markers found on the surface of red blood cells. These markers tell the body which blood type the cells belong to. A simpler way to put this is: 'What are the surface markers on blood?'
asks: Are antigens like labels on blood cells?

faq.a: A transfusion is the medical process of giving donated blood to a person who needs it. This is done to replace lost blood volume or components. You might ask: 'How is blood given to someone?'
asks: What is donated blood used for?
Why do people need blood transfusions?

facts: Blood groups are determined by antigens on red blood cells.
Type O blood is the universal donor because it lacks A and B antigens.
Type AB blood is the universal recipient because it has both A and B antigens.
Transfusions must match blood types to prevent dangerous reactions.

quiz.say: If a person has Type A blood, what antigens are present on their red blood cells?
quiz.why: Type A blood is defined by the presence of the A antigen on its cells.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the presence of Antigen B would make the blood Type B or AB.
wrong.1: This is wrong because 'no antigens' describes Type O blood, not Type A.
wrong.2: This is wrong because having both antigens defines Type AB blood.

quiz.say: Which blood type can safely receive blood from any other type?
quiz.why: Type AB has both A and B antigens, allowing it to accept blood from any source.

wrong.0: Type A can only safely receive blood from Type A or Type O donors.
wrong.1: Type B cannot safely receive blood from Type A donors.
wrong.3: Type O is the universal donor, meaning it can give blood, not receive it safely.
